objects: source and target ancestry effects; LD patterns
assumptions: Source and target ancestries have different LD patterns and possibly heterogeneous effects.
conclusion: Source-ancestry effect estimates can be biased for the target ancestry, motivating adaptation using target sample data.
scope: Cross-ancestry prediction; a motivating statement rather than a bias theorem.
span: However, due to different LD patterns and possible effect-size heterogeneity across ancestries, effect-size estimation from the source ancestry can result in biased estimators of effect sizes in the target ancestry. To adapt the model to the target population and achieve better prediction performance, we borrow the idea of transfer learning and attempt to combine information from the baseline model and the target sample data.

objects: Y; G; beta=beta_pre+tau; C; gamma; epsilon; squared-error loss
assumptions: A pre-trained coefficient vector is supplied; C includes an intercept.
conclusion: The target phenotype is modeled as an additive genotype-plus-covariate regression with effects decomposed into source effects plus target adjustments, fitted by squared-error minimization.
scope: Target regression; this passage does not specify a noise distribution.
span: Specifically, for the target ancestry group, we have the following model: Y = ∑ j = 1 M G_{j} β_{j} + C γ + ε = ∑ j = 1 M G_{j} ( β_{j}^{p r e} + τ_{j} ) + C γ + ε , where β_{j} is the true effect size of the target ancestry group, assumed to be unknown; β_{j}^{p r e} is given by the pre-trained model; τ_{j} is the difference between β_{j}^{p r e} and β_{j}; C is the covariate matrix including the intercept; and γ is a vector of covariate coefficients. Our goal is to minimize the following loss function: L o s s = ( Y − ∑ j = 1 M G_{j} β_{j} − C γ )^{2} .

conclusion: The pre-trained source model is treated as prior knowledge for predicting target-ancestry genetic effects.
scope: Prior knowledge is supplied through coefficient initialization in the fitting algorithm.
span: Supposing that we have pre-trained a PRS model using GWAS summary statistics from a source ancestry, this model could be considered as prior knowledge to predict the genetic effects in the target ancestry.

objects: beta^(r); beta_pre; alpha; G^T(Y-G beta-C gamma)
assumptions: The squared-error target regression is used and source-model coefficients initialize the iterations.
conclusion: TL-PRS updates the effect vector by gradient descent from the pre-trained coefficients, with learning rate alpha=2 alpha-prime.
scope: Equation 1 is an update rule, not a convergence or prediction guarantee.
span: Since the second derivative is constantly larger than 0, we can perform a gradient descent algorithm on β_{j} with the initial value β_{j}^{p r e}. Given the current estimate β_{j}^{( r )} in the r-th iteration, the next value, i.e., β_{j}^{( r + 1 )} is β_{j}^{( r + 1 )} = β_{j}^{( r )} − α^{′} (∂ L o s s)/(∂ β_{j}) = β_{j}^{( r )} + 2 α^{′} G_{j}^{T} ( Y − G β^{( r )} − C γ ) , (Equation 1) and we define the learning rate α = 2 α^{′}.

objects: target GWAS summary statistics; G^T Y; G^T G; target-ancestry reference genotypes
assumptions: Target-ancestry GWAS summary statistics are available when individual-level training data are inaccessible.
conclusion: TL-PRS can fit from target summary statistics by estimating G-transpose-Y from those statistics and G-transpose-G from a target-ancestry public reference dataset.
scope: Summary-based training uses reference-estimated LD; individual-level tuning is the default.
span: When the individual-level data from the training sample are not accessible, TL-PRS can still be applied if GWAS summary statistics of the target ancestry are available. In the step of model fitting, G^{T} Y can be estimated by the summary statistics of the target ancestry,5 and G^{T} G can be estimated by the target ancestry using a public reference dataset, such as the 1000 Genomes Project. In the step of hyper-parameter tuning, the approach of using individual-level data is applied in default.

objects: PRS_i; estimated effects beta_hat_j; genotype G_ij
assumptions: Estimated genetic effects and individual genotypes are available.
conclusion: The polygenic score is the sum of genotype values weighted by estimated genetic effects.
scope: Generic PRS definition used by the paper, including TL-PRS scores.
span: With GWAS summary statistics (i.e., the effect-size estimate and standard error), a PRS is constructed as the summation of the estimated effects across all genetic variants on a given phenotype. For individual i, PRS can be defined as P R S_{i} = ∑ j = 1 M β ˆ_{j} G_{i j} , where M is the number of variants, G_{i j} is the genotype of the genetic variant j, and β ˆ_{j} is the effect size.

objects: baseline coefficients from Lsum and PRS-CS
assumptions: The baseline PRS has been trained.
conclusion: TL-PRS can initialize its target-ancestry gradient descent using baseline effects from existing PRS methods, including PRS-CS and Lassosum.
scope: Baseline effects are adapted; the baseline method is not asserted to be equivalent to TL-PRS.
span: TL-PRS can use PRSs from any existing PRS methods (such as Lsum and PRS-CS) as a baseline model. Using the effect sizes of the baseline model as initial values, TL-PRS iterates the gradient descent algorithm to adapt the effect sizes for the target ancestry group.

assumptions: Two ancestry-specific PRSs have been constructed from different GWAS summary statistics.
conclusion: The multi-source initializer is a weighted sum pi PRS_1+(1-pi) PRS_2 with pi in [0,1], selected by cross-validation.
scope: Defines the two-source combination used for MTL-PRS initialization.
span: Supposing two PRSs, P R S_{1} and P R S_{2}, are constructed from two different GWAS summary statistics, then the cross-population PRS can be built as P R S = π P R S_{1} + ( 1 − π ) P R S_{2} , where π is a tuning parameter with range [0,1] and can be decided using the cross-validation method.9

assumptions: Genetic correlation between source and target ancestries is large.
conclusion: When source-target genetic correlations are large, baseline methods may already suffice and TL-PRS may not improve prediction.
scope: Author discussion of performance dependence; no universal improvement guarantee.
span: Overall, the performance of TL-PRS depends on many factors, such as target ancestries and trait types. When genetic correlations between source and target ancestries are large, the baseline methods are sufficient for prediction, and TL-PRS might not further improve the prediction performance.

objects: PRS-CSx; linear combinations of ancestry-specific coefficient vectors
assumptions: The cross-population predictor is a linear combination of two ancestry-specific PRSs.
conclusion: The paper describes PRS-CSx as using linear combinations of two PRS-CS scores and warns that optimal prediction effects need not be such a combination and that this strategy requires more than one ancestry summary source.
scope: Authors characterization of an earlier method motivating target-specific adaptation.
span: PRS-CSx10 implemented the same linear-combination approach using two PRSs trained with PRS-CS. However, this linear-combination approach implicitly assumes that the optimal effect sizes (or beta coefficients) weighting for prediction are a linear combination of the effect sizes of two PRSs, which may not hold in all situations. In addition, this method cannot be used when GWAS summary statistics are available for only one ancestry.
